section_summary: This section opens with the end of one signature list and then contains Donald H. Gibbs’s covering letter, an anti-armament resolution, and dozens of pages of signatures from Illinois Methodist clergy and young people urging reduced military spending and an end to shipments of war materials to East Asia. Subsequent correspondence from Methodist officials, church groups, and private citizens similarly protests American exports to Japan, while State Department replies explain the Neutrality Act, the President’s decision not to invoke it, arms-export licensing totals for China and Japan, and official opposition to bombing civilians. The section also includes a Hong Kong consular despatch reporting Eugene Chen’s criticism of American assistance to Japan and ends with a Presbyterian mission official forwarding an appeal from Canton against Japanese bombing.

subfiles.title: Continuation of an Illinois petition signature list
subfiles.from: Illinois petition signatories
subfiles.about: Continuation of a list of Illinois residents supporting a petition concerning American policy and war supplies in East Asia.
subfiles.summary: These pages consist almost entirely of names and Illinois towns and are plainly the concluding portion of a document begun before page 543. Several signatories reappear in the later Old Salem resolution lists, indicating related Methodist peace activism.

subfiles.title: Donald H. Gibbs transmits the Old Salem resolution
subfiles.from: Donald H. Gibbs, Dean, Old Salem Epworth League Institute
subfiles.about: Transmits a petition from Illinois Methodist ministers and young people seeking changes in armament and munitions-export policy.
subfiles.summary: Gibbs explains that Methodist young people and ministers have spent a week studying national and international affairs. On behalf of these Illinois Christian youth leaders, he asks the President to reduce armaments and change the policy permitting continued exports of war materials to the Orient.

subfiles.title: Old Salem Epworth League Institute resolution and signatures
subfiles.from: Faculty and students of the Old Salem Epworth League Institute, Illinois Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Calls for reduced American armament expenditure and an end to exports of gasoline, oil, scrap iron, aircraft, ammunition, and other war supplies to the Orient.
subfiles.summary: The resolution deplores the killing and destruction in China and regrets the American role in teaching warfare and providing implements and munitions to both China and Japan. It declares war an improper means of settling international disputes and asks the President and Congress to reduce domestic armament spending and stop shipments of war materials to East Asia. The remainder consists of extensive signature sheets listing hundreds of Illinois supporters and their towns.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Donald H. Gibbs
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Old Salem resolutions and explains why the Neutrality Act has not been invoked against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Gibbs for the resolutions and encloses the President’s January 28, 1938 message, the May 1, 1937 Joint Resolution, and a pamphlet on international traffic in arms. He explains that an arms embargo would follow only if the President formally found that a state of war existed, and that the law does not permit prohibition of commodities other than enumerated arms and implements of war. The President has concluded that invoking the statute in the Far Eastern conflict would not serve the broad interests of the United States and its nationals.

subfiles.title: Bishop Charles Wesley Flint protests shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Charles Wesley Flint
subfiles.about: Urges the President to end American sales and shipments that sustain Japan’s undeclared war on China.
subfiles.summary: Flint states that many, if not all, Americans are distressed by sales and shipments to Japan during its undeclared and ruthless war upon China. He respectfully asks the President to use his powers to terminate the traffic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Bishop Flint
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal limits on prohibiting exports to Japan and supplies comparative arms-license figures for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that only a presidential finding of a state of war would activate the Neutrality Act’s embargo, which would apply to both China and Japan. It says the President has decided that invocation would not serve American interests. The Department reports that since July 1, 1937 it had licensed $13,973,682.85 in arms exports to China and $10,376,214.93 to Japan.

subfiles.title: Ruth A. Sherrill demands an end to exports usable by Japan
subfiles.from: Ruth A. Sherrill
subfiles.about: Calls for an embargo on anything convertible into instruments of destruction and describes reported Japanese atrocities at Nanjing.
subfiles.summary: Sherrill argues that Congress has failed to respond to Japan’s war on China or to defend treaty obligations supporting China’s integrity. Speaking after a Chinese-relief “bowl of rice” dinner, she demands that the United States refuse to ship Japan anything usable for warfare. She recounts reports of burning and bayoneting prisoners and civilians, rape, looting, destruction, and violations of the foreign safety zone during the fall of Nanjing, while praising reciprocal trade agreements as a possible instrument of peace.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Ruth A. Sherrill
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Sherrill’s embargo request with the Department’s Neutrality Act position and arms-export figures.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, but that no authority exists to embargo Japan alone in its absence. He reiterates the President’s judgment that invoking the Joint Resolution would not serve the country’s broad interests. The response provides export-license values and welcomes Sherrill’s support for reciprocal trade agreements as a contribution to peace.

subfiles.title: Atlanta Methodist superintendents’ letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: J. F. Demery, E. G. Newton, and J. W. Queen
subfiles.about: Protests continued arms and munitions shipments to Japan on behalf of the Atlanta Methodist Conference.
subfiles.summary: Three district superintendents write for clergy and laity representing more than 25,000 members and constituents. Shocked by the deaths of women, children, and other noncombatants, they ask the President to use his good offices to halt American shipments of war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Atlanta Methodist superintendents’ letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: J. F. Demery, E. G. Newton, and J. W. Queen
subfiles.about: Sends the Secretary of State the Atlanta Conference’s protest against war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This is a counterpart of the letter sent to President Roosevelt, addressed directly to Secretary Hull. The superintendents cite the Conference’s constituency of more than 25,000 and ask Hull to help halt shipments after widespread civilian deaths in China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. F. Demery
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s legal position on an embargo, gives export-license totals, and cites condemnation of aerial bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges the Atlanta Conference’s request and encloses the May 1, 1937 Joint Resolution. He explains that an embargo under the Neutrality Act would require a presidential war finding and would then apply to both belligerents, while the President has judged invocation contrary to broad American interests. The letter reports licensed arms exports of $13,973,682.85 to China and $10,376,214.93 to Japan and points to the Secretary of State’s June 11 statements against supplying aeronautical equipment to countries bombing civilian populations.

subfiles.title: Supplementary acknowledgment to J. F. Demery
subfiles.from: Edgar Allen, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the copy referred by the White House and directs Demery to the Department’s earlier response.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges, through a White House referral, Demery’s July 25 request for an embargo on war-material exports to Japan. Rather than repeat the substantive answer, it refers him to the Department’s August 8 response concerning the same matter.

subfiles.title: White House referral of the Worcester Methodist communication
subfiles.from: M. H. McIntyre, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Refers a communication concerning Far Eastern policy to the State Department for consideration and acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: McIntyre forwards the accompanying Worcester Methodist appeal to the State Department. The brief memorandum requests both consideration and acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: John L. Cairns forwards a Worcester Methodist resolution
subfiles.from: John L. Cairns
subfiles.about: Urges action against trade with Japan that sustains the Far Eastern conflict and destroys friendly relations.
subfiles.summary: Cairns reports that a large, well-attended meeting representing men’s Bible classes in the Worcester District’s churches adopted the stated position. He asks Roosevelt to do everything in his power to end traffic between the United States and Japan that sustains the conflict and destroys lives, property, and long-standing friendship.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to John L. Cairns
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Worcester resolution and explains the Neutrality Act and current arms-export licensing.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Cairns for providing the resolution and encloses the Joint Resolution and a pamphlet on international arms traffic. He explains that the President cannot prohibit non-arms commodities under the statute and has declined to invoke its arms embargo because doing so would not serve the nation’s broad interests. Updated figures list $14,165,130.98 in licensed arms exports to China and $10,450,757.93 to Japan since July 1, 1937.

subfiles.title: Marshfield Hills citizen protests assistance to Japan
subfiles.from: Mrs. Joseph M. Flamand
subfiles.about: Asks whether the government can restrain Americans from supplying Japan with bombing aircraft and munitions materials.
subfiles.summary: The writer describes herself as a plain citizen troubled that Americans are supplying Japan with bombing planes and materials for ammunition. She calls such assistance to Japan’s bullying of China a national disgrace and adds her protest to those already voiced by many other citizens.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Flamand
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits on export controls, provides arms-license totals, and restates official opposition to bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: The Department replies that the Neutrality Act would bar arms exports to both China and Japan only after a presidential finding of war and cannot be used to prohibit other commodities. It reiterates the President’s decision that invocation would not serve American interests and reports licenses worth $14,165,130.98 for China and $10,450,757.93 for Japan. Yost also recalls the Secretary of State’s public condemnation of bombing civilian populations and of its material encouragement, particularly by manufacturers of bombing aircraft.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 232: Eugene Chen’s criticism of American war-material supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: Addison E. Southard, American Consul General, Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Reports Eugene Chen’s public accusation that American commerce, credit, and arms sales assist Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Southard quotes Chen as saying that Japanese weapons supplied partly by American manufacturers had killed or wounded more than a million Chinese and displaced 150 million, while American purchases, credit, and arms sales objectively assisted the invasion. The consul then discusses Chen’s recent return from Europe, his hopes for office in the Central Chinese or Canton governments, and the activities of his sons Percy and Jack. British intelligence officials suspect Chen’s quiet life in Kowloon is temporary and that he is seeking a route back into Chinese or international politics.

subfiles.title: Bishop James Chamberlain Baker protests war-sustaining trade with Japan
subfiles.from: James Chamberlain Baker
subfiles.about: Urges the Secretary to end American trade supplying Japan with the sinews of war.
subfiles.summary: Baker says that many Americans are disturbed because the United States is furnishing Japan with the means to continue war. He asks the Secretary to do everything possible to end this traffic and states that the hundreds of churches under his episcopal oversight would strongly support that position.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Bishop Baker
subfiles.from: Counselor, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Baker’s protest by outlining the Neutrality Act, presidential discretion, and current arms-export totals.
subfiles.summary: The response explains that a presidential war proclamation would trigger an arms embargo against both China and Japan, while no authority exists to embargo Japan alone or to prohibit commodities outside the statutory arms list. It says the President has concluded that invocation would not serve the interests of the United States and its people. The letter reports licensed exports since July 1, 1937 of $14,165,130.98 to China and $10,450,757.93 to Japan.

subfiles.title: Presbyterian Board forwards Canton bombing appeal
subfiles.from: Lloyd S. Ruland, China Secretary, Board of Foreign Missions of the Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A.
subfiles.about: Forwards A. J. Fisher’s cable reporting renewed Japanese bombing of Canton and personally advocates refusing war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ruland transmits Fisher’s cable stating that Japan has resumed large-scale bombing of Canton without regard to legitimate objectives, causing terrible civilian suffering that will continue unless Japan is restrained. Although the Board cannot take formal action until September, Ruland says he and consulted colleagues believe protests should now be reinforced by refusing to sell Japan the materials used in its invasion of China.
